transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-07-23 15:00 PDT — duration ~62m
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Leah Morgan (FinOptima PL), Omar Sheikh (FinOptima ML Infra), Priya Desai (FinOptima Security), Tom Keller (FinOptima CTO)
Recording ID: ff-20250723-0192

Summary (auto): quick notes above.

[00:00] Avery: okay, hi everyone, thanks for making time. quick intro — i m avery, i'll run today. diego from the se team will deep dive on the runtime stuff.
[00:15] Leah: hey thanks, we've got a tight agenda. trade desk is spiking unpredictable traffic between 09:30 and 10:00 UTC sometimes, so isolation is top of mind.
[00:25] Diego: got it. we'll cover how dedicated capacity + capacity fencing works and the fallback policies to hosted when dedicated hits limits. i'll also show KV cache behavior and batching tradeoffs.
[00:40] Omar: random note — we saw a noisy neighbor event on vendor X last quarter, 40% increased latency for our short-ttl reqs, so we want hard guarantees or good fallbacks.
[00:55] Priya: also sec — encryption/KMS and audit logs are requirements. on-prem might be needed for some data flows.
[01:05] Diego: noted. quick outline: 1) isolation primitives and how we fence GPUs; 2) request routing and graceful fallback; 3) batching and p99 effects; 4) KV / prefix cache effects on throughput; 5) quantization experiments.

[04:15] Diego: starting with isolation — dedicated pools give reserved vGPU slots, pinned to tenant. capacity fencing means we enforce strict quotas at the scheduler layer, not best-effort. production: we run soft limits for autoscale but hard throttles for isolated pools.
[04:40] Leah: can you explain noisy neighbor protection? is that just QoS or actual runtime-level isolation?
[04:57] Diego: both. on infra we have cgroup/cuda-mig style isolation where available; at runtime we isolate model shards and memory so KV cache hits are local. that reduces interference on memory bandwidth. sometimes orchestration-level eviction still happens if temp disk / host oom.
[05:25] Tom: does that mean we can get an SLA for p95 latency under normal load? our SLAs with clients expect 200ms p95 for embeddings calls.
[05:40] Avery: for Dedicated we can map to an SLA tier. Diego: we have empirical profiles — small-embed jobs vs chat generation. p95 depends on sequence length and batching policy. we can guarantee throughput based on reserved gpus and a baseline batching config; p95 SLAs need a bit more specificity in the traffic profile.

[08:10] Diego: next, fallbacks. policy is: route to dedicated primary; if queue depth exceeds threshold or latency exceeds fallback latency, route to hosted variant (lower capacity but more pool capacity). we also support model-family fallbacks — e.g., 8-bit quant smaller variant. routing rules are pluggable with weights and can be time-windowed.
[08:45] Leah: what about consistency? we can't have different quality outputs for regulatory logs.
[08:52] Diego: good call. we surface 'variant_id' and 'model_hash' in logs and traces. also you can pin requests to only dedicated or disable fallbacks for certain endpoints. fallback is opt-in per route.

[10:05] Omar: curious about cold start behavior when fallback happens — do we pay warmup penalty? e g run_vm spinup?
[10:15] Diego: hosted has more warm instances generally; dedicated may scale from 0 to N in some configs. we recommend min-replicas >0 for latency-sensitive routes. prefix/KV cache can mitigate cold-start because if user prefixes are cached in external cache (or in local KV), the KV hit can avoid compute cost.

[12:30] Diego: on KV cache — two modes: per-tenant in-memory KV on the serving node (very low latency) and shared redis-style cache for cross-node. in dedicated pools we prefer local in-memory prefix caching so hit-rate is high.
[12:55] Leah: what's realistic hit-rate? for our use case, repeated spiky queries on similar prompts during market events.
[13:05] Diego: in our benchmarks with session-affine traffic we see 60-85% hit rates depending on cache size and prefix policy. for FinOptima's observed repeat-window (you mentioned ~30s bursts) a small LRU of size ~2-4k prefixes gets you 70% typically.
[13:30] Priya: are those prefixes stored encrypted at rest? we need KMS integration.
[13:36] Diego: yes for private/on-prem we use customer-managed KMS for cache encryption at rest and in-transit; in hosted we encrypt at rest with service-managed keys by default, and can bring-your-own-key via KMS for enterprise.

[15:00] Avery: switching to batching — continuous batching in our runtime aggregates requests up to a latency budget. there's a tradeoff: increase batch windows to raise throughput and GPU utilization, but p99 suffers for short queries.
[15:25] Omar: can we do adaptive batching per-route? we have both high-qps embedding endpoints and low-latency single-sentence inference.
[15:36] Diego: yep. we use workload-aware batching configs: per-route max_batch_size, target_latency_ms, and priority. also the runtime can preempt large batches for high-priority low-latency requests.
[15:50] Leah: any numbers you can share? like batch size vs p95 numbers for a 7B-like model?
[16:00] Diego: shallow numbers from our lab: unbatched single-token throughput ~15 tokens/s on A100-40GB for that family; with batch 16 we get ~220 tokens/s aggregated, but p95 tail increases by ~30-80ms depending on batching window. specific numbers are workload dependent. we'll run your exact payloads.

[19:40] Priya: quantization — we're nervous about 8-bit artifacts for legal text generation. do you support mixed precision? can we A/B produce and diff?
[19:52] Diego: yes. we support 8-bit and 4-bit quantizations, plus per-layer float fallback (mixed). you can run side-by-side inference and we have a diff tooling that computes embedding distance + ngram drift and a simple BLEU-style overlap for deterministic tests.
[20:20] Tom: do you observe hallucination increase with aggressive quant?
[20:25] Diego: sometimes for certain model families yes. that's why we recommend evals on a holdout prompt set. Redwood Optimize will suggest quant profiles by workload.

[22:00] Avery: back to isolation: if dedicated pool saturates we can either queue, start throttling, or fallback. what policy do you prefer?
[22:12] Leah: we prefer hard fencing for compliance except for non-sensitive endpoints where fallback is fine. can we make per-route rules?
[22:20] Diego: absolutely per-route. you can declare route attributes: "is_sensitive": true and that disables fallbacks and routes only to private/dedicated.

[24:00] Omar: network — if we deploy in VPC with private deployment, what's the hop for telemetry and how do you handle control-plane outages?
[24:12] Diego: private control plane can run in your VPC or as an air-gapped appliance. telemetry sinks are customer-managed — we push traces via your collector. control-plane outage fallback: nodes keep serving cached policy (store locally) for a TTL and keep accepting inference; management actions will queue until control plane recovers.

[26:45] Leah: weird edge case — during market open we have extreme short-lived concurrency spikes. if a long-running generation (e g batch story) occupies a GPU and blocks short reqs, how does Redwood mitigate that?
[26:58] Diego: runtime preemption: smaller requests get priority lanes. long runtimes are isolated to model-serving partitions where possible. we also offer bounded-max-latency queues where request will either be preempted or sent to fallback. that requires correct priority annotations.

[29:10] Tom: cost question — if we reserve dedicated and add min-replicas for low latency, cost goes up. is there a hybrid where we reserve baseline capacity and burst to hosted with fairly deterministic cost?
[29:25] Avery: yes hybrid is common. recommended pattern: reserve minimal dedicated for critical sensitive traffic and configure weighted fallback to hosted for overflow; billing shows per-use on hosted plus reserved amortized cost. we can model estimates if you share QPS.

[31:00] Diego: i pulled up a small simulation — hypothetical: 4 GPU dedicated pool, baseline traffic 120 qps embeddings, spikes to 900 qps for ~90s. with 4 GPUs and local KV cache, you'll hit 70% local cache and dedicated will handle ~60% of the work; the remainder falls back to hosted. tail latency under this config hit ~350ms p95 unless you increase min-replicas.
[31:40] Leah: 350ms p95 is high for some contracts. what if we bump min-replicas to 6?
[31:48] Diego: that drops p95 to ~180-220ms in the sim. cost model increases ~40%. we can show exact numbers with your payload.

[34:10] Omar: on the KV cache architecture, you mentioned local in-memory vs shared redis. if we have multi-AZ requirements and failover, how do you reconcile cache warms?
[34:22] Diego: multi-AZ — we prefer to have cache rehydrate from a shared durable store (redis or s3-backed) after failover. there's a warmup period; to avoid cold starts we keep a small pinned working set in each AZ if you enable cross-az replication for certain keys. it's a tradeoff: consistency vs memory duplication.

[36:00] Priya: security: what audit info is available per request? we need full request/response hash, model version, and user id mapping. also retention windows.
[36:12] Diego: request-level logs include model_hash, variant_id, route, response_time, and token counts. payloads are not logged by default; you can enable PII logging to a secure bucket for a short retention window. we also surface token-level cost breakdowns. retention policies configurable per-account.

[38:55] Leah: can you demonstrate the trace you mentioned — show an example where fallback happened and how we would see it in the console?
[39:05] Diego: sure we pulled a sample trace: (screen-share) — you can see hop: router -> dedicated pool -> decision to fallback -> hosted pool. logs show queue depth, decision metric and model hashes.
[40:25] (brief pause as Diego shares screen, some chatter)
[42:00] Diego: here's a captured scenario. note the latency spike and the fallback decision at t+1s. we annotate why: queue depth 94 and latency > target. you can tune the threshold.
[43:10] Tom: is there a safety mechanism so fallback won't cause data exfil because hosted is in different tenancy?
[43:25] Diego: yes — you can disable fallback for routes with sensitive data. additionally, for hosted fallback we only route anonymized payloads unless you explicitly allow raw input. also BYOK for hosted is available for enterprise where KMS wraps transit keys.

[45:10] Leah: operational playbook — during an incident what do we do? who's on-call?
[45:25] Avery: standard: Redwood SE will run a triage with your SREs, isolate pool, adjust fencing or increase min-replicas; emergency contract includes higher priority. we'll supply runbooks.

[47:30] Omar: for the bench we want you to run: 1) 7B chat model with our prompts; 2) embeddings for 512-length docs; compare float32 vs 8-bit quant and mixed; measure p50/p95/p99, KV-hit rates at 3 cache sizes; simulate our burst traffic shape.
[47:50] Avery: that's exactly what we'll do. Diego: i'll own the bench.

[49:00] Diego: little gotchas — streaming responses interact poorly with batching; if you have low-chunk streaming, batching window must be small else latency worse. also large-generation long-seqs lock KV resources longer.
[49:30] Leah: noted. also can you produce a config example for per-route policy?
[49:40] Diego: yes i'll send a yaml sample with route attrs: min_replicas, fallback: true/false, max_queue_ms, tenant_kv:local/redis, quant_profile:recommended.

[51:05] Priya: one more security point — can we get attestation for firmware/host images?
[51:15] Diego: for private/on-prem yes you can run attestations; for Dedicated hosted we provide image-signing and compliance docs; we can add SOC2/iso artifacts to the packet.

[53:20] Avery: quick recap and actions. next steps: run bench (Diego) and send results; AE sends pricing and SLA; customer provides traffic CSV and sensitive-route list.
[53:40] Leah: timeline — can we get the bench by next week?
[53:48] Diego: yes, target 2025-07-30.
[54:00] Tom: final Q: if dedicated fails over to hosted temporarily, what's the billing impact? are we double-billed?
[54:10] Avery: no double-billing — you pay reserved amortized monthly plus per-use for hosted overflow. we'll include modeled cost scenarios in the pricing sheet.

[56:00] (some cross-talk, wrap up)
[57:15] Priya: please include the security docs link in the follow up.
[57:25] Avery: will do. Diego: i'll attach bench config and results, plus a sample route yaml.
[58:12] Leah: thanks all. we'll sync after we see the bench.
[58:20] Session ended.
